items.front: Laws of indices: product, quotient, power-of-power, zero, negative, fractional?
items.back: a^{m} × a^{n} = a^{m+n}; a^{m} ÷ a^{n} = a^{m-n}; (a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}; a^{0} = 1; a^{-n} = 1 ÷ a^{n}; a^{m/n} = the n-th root of a, to the power m.
items.examPoint: Laws of indices — product, quotient and power-of-power

items.front: How do you solve an exponential equation like 7^{x-y} = 343?
items.back: Write both sides to the same base, then equate the exponents. Here 343 = 7^{3}, so x − y = 3.
items.examPoint: Exponential equations — solve for the unknown

items.front: Rationalise 1 ÷ (√3 − √2); and how do you compare surds?
items.back: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate √3 + √2: the bottom becomes 3 − 2 = 1, giving √3 + √2. Compare surds using a common index equal to the LCM of the root orders.

items.front: Log laws: product, quotient, power, change of base?
items.back: log(xy) = log x + log y; log(x/y) = log x − log y; log(x^{n}) = n × log x; log base a of b = (log b) ÷ (log a) in any common base.
items.examPoint: Logarithm laws — product, quotient, power and evaluation

items.front: Characteristic & mantissa; digits in a large power?
items.back: Characteristic = whole-number part = (digits − 1); mantissa = the positive decimal part. Digit count of N = characteristic of its base-10 log, plus 1.

items.front: HCF & LCM by prime factorization, and the product relation?
items.back: HCF = product of the lowest powers of common primes; LCM = product of the highest powers of all primes. For two numbers, A × B = HCF × LCM.
items.examPoint: Product of two numbers = HCF × LCM
items.source: APPSC Quantitative Reasoning — LCM and HCF

items.back: HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators ÷ LCM of denominators; LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators ÷ HCF of denominators.
items.source: APPSC Quantitative Reasoning — LCM and HCF

items.front: Remainder word-problem formulas (same remainder / constant gap)?
items.back: Smallest number with common remainder R = LCM + R. Greatest number dividing x, y, z with the same remainder = HCF of their differences. Constant (divisor − remainder) = k gives LCM − k.
items.examPoint: HCF and LCM — remainder and word problems
items.source: APPSC Quantitative Reasoning — LCM and HCF

items.front: HCF vs LCM: which word problems use which?
items.back: HCF: longest tape or tile, greatest equal distribution, fewest rows without mixing. LCM: bells or lights coinciding, runners meeting at the start, the least common number.
items.examPoint: LCM word problems — bells / lights coinciding
items.source: APPSC Quantitative Reasoning — LCM and HCF

items.front: Units digit of a power by cyclicity?
items.back: It depends only on the base's last digit; divide the exponent by 4 and use the remainder (remainder 0 means the last term). Cycle 7 is 7, 9, 3, 1, so 7^{105} gives 7.
items.source: APPSC Quantitative Reasoning — Cyclicity of Units Digit

items.front: Trailing zeros at the end of n factorial?
items.back: Count the power of 5: add the whole-number parts of n ÷ 5, n ÷ 25, n ÷ 125 and so on. For 100 factorial this is 20 + 4 + 0 = 24.
items.examPoint: Trailing zeros / power of a prime in a factorial
items.source: APPSC Quantitative Reasoning — Factorials / Power of a Prime
